concept.title: What is a Passkey?
concept.shortdesc: Describes passkeys as a form of cryptography that increases online security without using a password.

section.title: What is a Passkey?
section.p: For many users, passkeys are often easier than passwords. A passkey is a way to sign in to an account without typing a password.

Instead of relying only on something you know, like a password, passkeys use something you have (your phone, tablet, or computer), something you are (your fingerprint or face), or something you know (your device PIN). Some examples of passkeys include unlocking your phone with Face ID, tapping your fingerprint sensor, or entering your device PIN.
Under the hood, passkeys use advanced cryptography to keep your account secure. When you create a passkey, your device generates two digital keys:

ol.li: A public key, which is stored by the website or app.
A private key, which stays securely on your device.

section.note: The private key never leaves your device. When you log in, your device proves you’re really you by securely matching those keys together.

section.title: Why are Passkeys Secure?
section.p: Passkeys solve many of the biggest problems with passwords:

ul.li: There’s no password to steal: A common phishing attack tricks people into typing passwords into fake websites. But with passkeys, there’s usually no password to type.

Your secret key stays on your device: With passwords, websites store information that can potentially be stolen in a data breach. With passkeys, the sensitive private key stays on your personal device instead of sitting on a server.
Biometrics for the win: Even if someone steals your phone or laptop, they still typically need your fingerprint or face scan to use your passkey.

No more password reuse: Password reuse remains one of the biggest cybersecurity risks. If one account is breached, attackers often try the same password on other accounts. Passkeys remove that temptation because there’s no password to remember in the first place.
